newsitem.title: CANADA: CAW says GM Canada to delay economic package.
newsitem.headline: CAW says GM Canada to delay economic package.

text.p: The Canadian Auto Workers union said on Wednesday the Canadian unit of General Motors Corp delayed its plans to present its economic offer as expected at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT, ahead of tonight's midnight strike deadline.
CAW president Buzz Hargrove said GM Canada's chief negotiator, Dean Munger, informed the union early this morning that the company needed more time to review the offer.
Hargrove said talks recessed at about 0400 EDT/0800 GMT Wednesday after little progress on the key issue of outsourcing.
"I can't bargain both sides of the table," Hargrove said. "I told (Munger) I was ready to go all night, but he said they were going to bed."

Hargrove previously expressed frustration with the pace of the talks and GM's refusal to put an economic proposal on the table. With less than 24 hours before the 2359 EDT Wednesday/0359 GMT Thursday strike deadline, Hargrove said a strike appeared inevitable.
"We're not making any progress at all on the major issues," Hargrove said during a break in bargaining Tuesday night. "I'm not convinced that we can't avoid a strike here."
GM Canada spokesman Stew Low said the company was still working on its economic package.
"We'll get one to (Hargrove) as soon as we can," said Low.
If a deal cannot be reached, 26,000 GM workers will walk of the job over the next week under the union's escalating strike strategy.

Workers from Oshawa, Ontario and Ste-Therese, Quebec assembly plants would hit the picket lines at midnight tonight, followed by workers at Ontario parts plants in St. Catherines, Woodstock, Windsor and London, Ontario in the next week.

The major stumbling block remains GM's refusal to agree to the deal on outsourcing reached two weeks ago by the union and Chrysler Corp 's Canadian unit. That pact gave the union unprecedented say into future outsourcing decisions.

The union is also seeking to reverse GM's plans to sell or wind down three plants and outsource other work at a cost of about 5,500 jobs. GM has said it needs to outsource the work to remain competitive.
Hargrove denied speculation that friction within the union may lead to wildcat strikes before tonight's deadline.
In an internal bulletin to the membership, the union's chairman for the GM committee urged his members to stay on the job until the deadline.
"It is extremely important that the membership stay on the job until 11:59 p.m. tonight and then follow the escalating strike strategy," Dave Vyse said.
Hargrove acknowledged yesterday the local unions sometimes resist the direction of the CAW leadership.
"These guys don't go to obedience school," he said.
